Sensitivity Analysis: Studying a Design Before Collecting Data

Source: vignettes/sensitivity-analysis.Rmd
sensitivity-analysis.Rmd

Why Study a Design First

In a sequential procedure the final sample size is not chosen; it is whatever the data make it. The same is true of the width of the final confidence interval, which never exceeds the target but can fall below it, and of whether that interval contains the population value. Theory describes these only in the limit. As the target width narrows, the final sample size approaches the one a planner who knew the population values would have fixed in advance, and the coverage of the interval approaches the confidence level (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018, Lemma 3 and Theorem 2; 2019, Theorem 1). A particular study is not at the limit. A sensitivity analysis shows what the procedure does for one population value, one target, and one way of checking, by running the whole procedure many times on simulated data whose population value is known.

DMAR pairs most of its ss_aipe_*() fixed sample size planners with a sensitivity function (ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity() beside ss_aipe_smd(), for example), which shows what happens when a planning value is wrong. A sequential procedure has no planning value. Its sensitivity analysis shows what the stopping rule does in samples of the size the rule itself produces.

What Can Be Studied 

grep("^seq_.*_sensitivity$", ls("package:SMSD"), value = TRUE)
#>  [1] "seq_aipe_c_sensitivity"        "seq_aipe_cv_sensitivity"      
#>  [3] "seq_aipe_gini_sensitivity"     "seq_aipe_r_sensitivity"       
#>  [5] "seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity"       "seq_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity"
#>  [7] "seq_aipe_sm_sensitivity"       "seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity"     
#>  [9] "seq_budget_sensitivity"        "seq_mr_cv_sensitivity"        
#> [11] "seq_mr_smd_sensitivity"

Every sequential AIPE procedure has a sensitivity function, the contrast and the squared multiple correlation included; the one for the correlation studies the Pearson coefficient. The two minimum risk procedures, seq_mr_cv() and seq_mr_smd(), have one each, and so does the budget constrained procedure. The classical procedures for a mean have none; the section A Population of Your Own shows how to write the loop by hand, which is also the way to study Kendall’s tau, Spearman’s rho, or a population that the built in choices do not cover.

Each function does what a study would do: it draws the pilot sample, checks the stopping rule, adds observations, and checks again, until the rule is met. It does this G times and returns a summary.

One Call

A training program is to be compared with a control group, and the researcher wants a 95% confidence interval for the standardized mean difference. What should a study with a target width of 0.80 expect if the population value is 0.5?

smd <- seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 0.80, G = 100,
                                seed = 113)
smd
#> term                   value
#> true_value             0.5
#> target_width           0.8
#> conf_level             0.95
#> replications           100
#> mean_n                 49.97
#> median_n               49
#> sd_n                   3.534691
#> mean_width             0.7912251
#> median_width           0.7916159
#> pct_width_within       100
#> coverage               0.96
#> pct_hit_max_n          0
#> pct_variance_unusable  0

The rows are the same for every seq_aipe_*_sensitivity() function.

  • true_value, target_width, conf_level, replications: what was asked for.
  • mean_n, median_n, sd_n: the final sample size, per group for this effect size. A study like this one ends with about 50 per group, give or take a few. With the population values known, the sample size for this width would be 4 * qnorm(0.975)^2 / 0.80^2 * (2 + 0.5^2 / 4) = 49.5 per group for normal data, so the procedure spends almost nothing for not knowing them.
  • mean_width, median_width, pct_width_within: the width of the final interval, and the percentage of replications in which it was no wider than the target. That percentage is 100 whenever the stopping rule ended every replication.
  • coverage: the proportion of final intervals that contained the population value.
  • pct_hit_max_n: the percentage of replications that the cap max_n (100,000 by default) stopped before the rule was met. When it is above zero the other rows describe a truncated procedure.
  • pct_variance_unusable: the percentage of replications in which, at one or more checks, the variance estimate was zero, negative, or not finite, so that the rule was reported as not met there and sampling continued (vignette("seq-aipe-smd", package = "SMSD") shows such a check).

The result is an object of class smsd_sensitivity. It prints every value in fixed notation, and it is an ordinary data frame with columns term and value, so a number can be taken out by name. The one line function value_of() defined here does that in the rest of this vignette.

class(smd)
#> [1] "smsd_sensitivity" "data.frame"
smd$value[smd$term == "coverage"]
#> [1] 0.96

value_of <- function(out, term) out$value[out$term == term]
value_of(smd, "mean_n")
#> [1] 49.97

Every row is an estimate from G replications. The Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage of p is the square root of p(1 − p) / G:

mc_se <- function(out) {
  p <- value_of(out, "coverage")
  G <- value_of(out, "replications")
  sqrt(p * (1 - p) / G)
}
mc_se(smd)
#> [1] 0.01959592

With G = 100 the coverage above is known only to within about two standard errors, 0.039, either way. The runs in this vignette use a small G and wide targets so that it builds in seconds. Unless the text gives a standard error and draws a conclusion from it, they show how to read the output and are not evidence about the procedures. A result that will be reported deserves G = 10000, at the width the study will use, which puts the standard error of a coverage near 0.95 at about 0.002. At a narrow target such a run can take from minutes to an hour or more, and nothing is printed while it runs, so time a call with a small G first. The time grows with the final sample size and falls as batch rises, but a larger batch describes a study that checks less often (Checking in Batches), so use the batch size the study will use. The seed argument makes a run reproducible and leaves the caller’s random number stream as it found it.

Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, pp. 232–233, Tables 1 and 2) report simulations of this kind for the standardized mean difference, with one observation per group added at each stage and 5,000 replications, under the heading “Characteristics of the final sample size: An empirical demonstration.”

The other functions are called the same way, with two exceptions that follow from what they study. seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity() also takes the number of predictors, p, and is used below. seq_aipe_c_sensitivity() has no single population value to be given: it takes the population means of the groups, the contrast weights, and the population standard deviations (1 by default), and its true_value row is the contrast of the means. Here a new training format is compared with the average of two existing ones, the population contrast is half a standard deviation, and the target width is 1:

contrast <- seq_aipe_c_sensitivity(true_means = c(0.5, 0, 0),
                                   contrast_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),
                                   width = 1, G = 100, seed = 113)
contrast
#> term                   value
#> true_value             0.5
#> target_width           1
#> conf_level             0.95
#> replications           100
#> mean_n                 22.92
#> median_n               23
#> sd_n                   4.877655
#> mean_width             0.9654817
#> median_width           0.9682345
#> pct_width_within       100
#> coverage               0.94
#> pct_hit_max_n          0
#> pct_variance_unusable  0

The sample sizes in this summary are per group, and the width of a contrast is in the units of the response. The coverage row again rests on 100 replications; its standard error is 0.024.

Checking in Batches

By default the stopping rule is checked after every observation (per group, for a two group design), which is the purely sequential procedure of the articles. Few studies can do that. The batch argument is the number of observations added between checks, and a sensitivity analysis shows what checking less often costs.

batches <- c(10, 20)
runs <- lapply(batches, function(b) {
  seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 0.80, G = 100,
                           seed = 113, batch = b)
})
runs <- c(list(smd), runs)

overshoot <- sapply(runs, function(out) {
  c(mean_n = value_of(out, "mean_n"),
    mean_width = value_of(out, "mean_width"),
    coverage = value_of(out, "coverage"),
    se_coverage = mc_se(out))
})
colnames(overshoot) <- paste("batch", c(1, batches))
round(overshoot, 3)
#>             batch 1 batch 10 batch 20
#> mean_n       49.970   54.900   64.000
#> mean_width    0.791    0.758    0.701
#> coverage      0.960    0.930    0.940
#> se_coverage   0.020    0.026    0.024

A study that checks only after every batch cannot stop between checks, so it ends with more observations and a somewhat narrower interval. Here the mean final sample size per group rises from 50.0 with a check after every observation to 64.0 with a check after every 20. The coverage row cannot separate the three designs: its entries differ by at most 0.030, and each has a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.020 to 0.026 (the last row). In larger runs at a target width of 0.4 the mean final sample size per group was 199.1, 201.2, 203.6, and 209.5 for batches of 1, 5, 10, and 20, about half a batch more per group, and coverage stayed between 0.949 and 0.952 (4,700 to 6,000 replications each; ?seq_aipe_sensitivity).

Reading the Coverage Row

The width of the final interval is guaranteed. Its coverage is not: the articles prove that coverage approaches the confidence level as the target narrows, and say nothing about any particular width. Whether a target is narrow enough depends on the effect size, on the population value, and on the distribution of the data.

For a standardized mean difference of 0.5 and normal data, even the wide target used above is narrow enough: with many more replications the coverage at a width of 0.8 was 0.95 (?seq_aipe_sensitivity; the row is in the table below). The same design with right skewed data is a different matter. The argument distribution = "skewed" draws both groups from a chi square distribution with 3 degrees of freedom, shifted and scaled so that the means and the variance are those of the normal case. This run checks after every five participants per group, which keeps 1,000 replications quick:

skewed <- seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 0.80,
                                   distribution = "skewed", G = 1000,
                                   seed = 113, batch = 5)
round(c(mean_n = value_of(skewed, "mean_n"),
        coverage = value_of(skewed, "coverage"),
        se_coverage = mc_se(skewed)), 3)
#>      mean_n    coverage se_coverage 
#>      52.285       0.925       0.008

The coverage is 0.925, which is 3.0 standard errors below the 0.95 that was asked for, more than Monte Carlo error accounts for. The interval is as narrow as requested, but it contains the population value somewhat less often than its confidence level says.

At narrower targets the shortfall under skew is much smaller, though at a width of 0.4 it has not vanished: coverage was 0.944 at a width of 0.4 and 0.949 at 0.2, against 0.952 and 0.946 for normal data (?seq_aipe_smd). The verification study in vignette("complete-tour", package = "SMSD"), with 10,000 replications for each of the population values 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 at a width of 0.4, found 0.942 to 0.946 for skewed data and 0.949 to 0.951 for normal data: about half a percentage point short of 0.95 under skew, which is more than Monte Carlo error.

In the other direction, coverage is lower again at a target wider still, for normal data as well, and the more so the larger the population value. A design at the wide end deserves a run of its own under each population that is plausible.

For a correlation, a target half as wide as the one above may not be narrow enough even with normal data. This study of a correlation of 0.4 checks after every five pairs:

r <- seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(true_value = 0.4, width = 0.4, G = 100,
                            seed = 113, batch = 5)
r
#> term                   value
#> true_value             0.4
#> target_width           0.4
#> conf_level             0.95
#> replications           100
#> mean_n                 62.25
#> median_n               60
#> sd_n                   22.64543
#> mean_width             0.3714632
#> median_width           0.3826196
#> pct_width_within       100
#> coverage               0.82
#> pct_hit_max_n          0
#> pct_variance_unusable  12

In this run 82 of the 100 final intervals contained the population correlation, a coverage of 0.820 with a standard error of 0.038 where 0.95 was asked for, and in 12 percent of the replications the variance estimate was unusable at some check. A run of this size cannot give the second decimal place, but the shortfall is real: with one pair added at a time and many more replications, the coverage at this population value and width is 0.78 (the third row of the table below). The reason is the estimate of the asymptotic variance in small samples. It is a combination of ratios of sample moments that tends to run low when the sample is small, so the rule is met too early and the interval is too narrow (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2019, Appendix D, p. 514).

The table collects what these functions measured for the standardized mean difference and for some of the harder cases, at a 95% confidence level with the default settings and normal data unless a distribution is named. It is taken from ?seq_aipe_sensitivity, where the replication counts and standard errors are given (each row rests on 800 to 34,000 replications).

Effect size and population value Target width Mean final n Coverage Percent of replications with an unusable variance estimate
Standardized mean difference, 0.5 0.8 51 0.95 below 0.1
Standardized mean difference, 0.5 0.4 199 0.95 0.0
Correlation, 0.4 0.4 55 0.78 16.5
Correlation, 0.4 0.2 263 0.93 0.9
Correlation, 0.4 0.1 1,079 0.95 0.0
Correlation, 0.9 0.1 75 0.45 79.5
Correlation, 0.9 0.025 819 0.90 1.3
Regression slope, 0.5 0.4 80 0.83 20.1
Regression slope, 0.5 0.2 377 0.94 1.3
Regression slope, 2 0.2 217 0.61 65.3
Coefficient of variation, 0.5, lognormal 0.2 62 0.79 0.0
Coefficient of variation, 0.5, lognormal 0.05 1,561 0.90 0.0
Gini index, 0.3 0.2 30 0.89 0.0

Three things in the table matter for planning.

First, coverage depends on the population value as well as on the width. A width of 0.1 is ample for a correlation of 0.4 and far from enough for a correlation of 0.9, because a strong correlation is estimated with so little sampling error that the rule is met in a small sample. Run the analysis at every population value that is plausible for the study, the strongest included.

Second, the remedies are a narrower target, a larger minimum pilot sample (m_0), or both. With m_0 = 40 at a width of 0.4, coverage for a correlation of 0.4 rose from 0.78 to 0.90 while the mean final sample size rose from 55 to 64, and coverage for a slope of 0.5 rose from 0.83 to 0.92. A larger pilot is a weaker remedy when the relationship is strong: for a correlation of 0.9 at a width of 0.1, m_0 = 100 raised coverage only from 0.45 to 0.69.

Third, an unusable variance estimate at an early check is not the problem itself; the check functions report the rule as not met there and sampling continues. It is a sign that the samples the rule is working with are small for this effect size, and the estimate on which a replication finally stops can still be too low. When the relationship is very strong the estimate can also stay unusable for a long time, so set max_n when exploring such conditions and read pct_hit_max_n.

Several Conditions in One Table: The Squared Multiple Correlation

The summaries are data frames, so a table over conditions takes a few lines. For the squared multiple correlation the condition that matters most is the number of predictors. The function generates multivariate normal data, the assumption under which that procedure is derived; p is the number of predictors.

predictors <- c(2, 5, 10)
r2_runs <- lapply(predictors, function(p) {
  seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity(true_value = 0.50, width = 0.30, p = p, G = 200,
                          seed = 113)
})
data.frame(
  predictors = predictors,
  mean_n = sapply(r2_runs, value_of, "mean_n"),
  coverage = sapply(r2_runs, value_of, "coverage"),
  se_coverage = sapply(r2_runs, mc_se)
)
#>   predictors mean_n coverage se_coverage
#> 1          2  84.39    0.880  0.02297825
#> 2          5  81.97    0.870  0.02378024
#> 3         10  72.47    0.705  0.03224709

The stopping rule asks for no more observations when there are more predictors, and the coverage falls: the sample squared multiple correlation overestimates the population value by more the more predictors there are, and the rule does not correct for it. The standard errors in the last column are large because G is small, but the trend is not a Monte Carlo accident. With 10,000 replications per condition the coverage at this population value and width was 0.900 with 2 predictors, 0.845 with 5, 0.668 with 10, and 0.361 with 15 (?seq_aipe_R2). vignette("seq-aipe-correlations", package = "SMSD") discusses what to do about it.

Minimum Risk

The minimum risk procedures (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2016, 2017) have no interval and no coverage. Their sensitivity functions compare the procedure with the best fixed sample size, the one that would minimize the risk if the population value were known. For a standardized mean difference of 0.5, a price of 8,000 per unit of squared error, and a cost of 4 per participant:

mr <- seq_mr_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, A = 8000, c = 4, G = 200,
                             seed = 113)
mr
#> term                value
#> true_value          0.5
#> loss_A              8000
#> cost_1              4
#> cost_2              4
#> replications        200
#> optimal_n1          45.41476
#> optimal_n2          45.41476
#> minimum_risk        726.6361
#> mean_n1             50.635
#> mean_n2             50.635
#> median_n1           51
#> median_n2           51
#> sd_n1               0.6958419
#> sd_n2               0.6958419
#> ratio_n1            1.114946
#> ratio_n2            1.114946
#> mean_estimate       0.5020693
#> mean_risk           726.8934
#> risk_efficiency     1.000354
#> se_risk_efficiency  0.04153699
#> regret              0.257265
#> pct_hit_max_n       0

The rows to read are ratio_n1 and ratio_n2, the mean final sample size of each group over the optimal one, and risk_efficiency, the mean realized loss over the minimum risk, with its Monte Carlo standard error in the next row. Each should be near 1. Here the procedure takes about 11 percent more than the optimal 45.4 per group, because the correction term in its stopping rule guards against stopping too early, and its risk efficiency is 1.000 (standard error 0.042): the risk is nearly flat around its minimum, so the extra observations cost little. seq_mr_cv_sensitivity() reports the same quantities for the coefficient of variation, with one row where the two group function has two: cost, optimal_n, mean_n, median_n, sd_n, and ratio_n. Both functions take batch.

A Budget

seq_budget_sensitivity() runs the budget constrained procedure of Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025) for population means, standard deviations, costs, and a budget that the user supplies. It adds one observation at a time to the group that seq_budget_next() names, so it has no batch argument. Here a new training format is compared with the average of two existing ones; the population contrast is 2, and a noninferiority margin of 5 is of interest.

budget <- seq_budget_sensitivity(
  true_means = c(52, 50, 50),
  true_sds = c(9, 6, 6),
  contrast_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),
  cost_per_group = c(38, 15, 10),
  budget = 1500,
  margin = 5,
  G = 200,
  seed = 113,
  m_0 = 10
)
budget
#> term                           value
#> true_contrast                  2
#> budget                         1500
#> conf_level                     0.95
#> replications                   200
#> coverage                       0.93
#> mean_total_cost                1490.24
#> sd_total_cost                  8.400311
#> pct_within_budget              100
#> pct_rule_met                   0
#> mean_n_1                       28.23
#> mean_n_2                       15.22
#> mean_n_3                       18.92
#> optimal_n_1                    28.59535
#> optimal_n_2                    15.17121
#> optimal_n_3                    18.58086
#> mean_estimated_variance        3.721556
#> mean_true_variance             3.989493
#> empirical_variance             4.425726
#> optimal_variance               3.910227
#> margin                         5
#> alpha_level                    0.05
#> noninferiority_rejection_rate  0.975

The summary answers the questions a budget raises. How much of it is spent: mean_total_cost, and pct_within_budget, which is 100 by construction. How sampling ends: pct_rule_met is the percentage of replications in which every group reached its criterion, and in the rest the budget could not pay for another needed observation, which is the usual ending. How close the allocation comes to the best one: the mean_n_ rows beside the optimal_n_ rows, and mean_true_variance beside optimal_variance. How well the interval and the test perform: coverage, with a standard error here of 0.018, and noninferiority_rejection_rate, which is the power of the noninferiority test at this margin because the population contrast is above the negative of the margin.

A Population of Your Own

The sensitivity functions generate data from a few named populations. When the population of interest is not among them, or the procedure has no sensitivity function, the loop is short to write, because the check functions do all of the work. The example is a standardized mean difference between two groups rated on a 7 point scale: discrete, bounded, and skewed in opposite directions in the two groups.

p_control <- c(0.10, 0.20, 0.25, 0.20, 0.12, 0.08, 0.05)
p_program <- rev(p_control)

rating_mean <- function(p) sum(1:7 * p)
rating_var <- function(p) sum((1:7 - rating_mean(p))^2 * p)
true_delta <- (rating_mean(p_program) - rating_mean(p_control)) /
  sqrt((rating_var(p_program) + rating_var(p_control)) / 2)
true_delta
#> [1] 0.6487847

one_study <- function(width = 0.80, batch = 10) {
  m <- seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = width)
  program <- sample(7, m, replace = TRUE, prob = p_program)
  control <- sample(7, m, replace = TRUE, prob = p_control)
  repeat {
    out <- seq_aipe_smd(program, control, width = width)
    if (attr(out, "is_satisfied")) break
    program <- c(program, sample(7, batch, replace = TRUE, prob = p_program))
    control <- c(control, sample(7, batch, replace = TRUE, prob = p_control))
  }
  summary(out)
}

set.seed(113)
studies <- do.call(rbind, replicate(100, one_study(), simplify = FALSE))
covered <- with(studies, lower_limit <= true_delta & true_delta <= upper_limit)
c(mean_n = mean(studies$current_n), coverage = mean(covered))
#>   mean_n coverage 
#>    61.60     0.97

summary() turns each final check into one row, so the replications stack into a data frame with one row per simulated study. The coverage of 0.970 rests on 100 studies and has a standard error of about 0.017. A loop for Kendall’s tau or Spearman’s rho through seq_aipe_r() has the same shape.

So does a loop for a classical procedure, none of which has a sensitivity function. The purely sequential fixed width interval for a normal mean, seq_fwd_norm_mean(), takes the half width d. With a half width of 0.5 and a population standard deviation of 2, a planner who knew the standard deviation would take (qnorm(0.975) * 2 / 0.5)2 = 61.5 observations.

one_mean_study <- function(d = 0.5, mu = 10, sigma = 2) {
  x <- rnorm(seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d = d), mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  repeat {
    out <- seq_fwd_norm_mean(x, d = d)
    if (attr(out, "is_satisfied")) break
    x <- c(x, rnorm(1, mean = mu, sd = sigma))
  }
  summary(out)
}

set.seed(113)
mean_studies <- do.call(rbind, replicate(100, one_mean_study(),
                                         simplify = FALSE))
mean_covered <- with(mean_studies, lower_limit <= 10 & 10 <= upper_limit)
c(mean_n = mean(mean_studies$current_n), coverage = mean(mean_covered))
#>   mean_n coverage 
#>    59.25     0.89

The 100 studies ended with 59.2 observations on average, and 0.890 of their intervals contained the population mean (standard error 0.031). The confidence level of this procedure is asymptotic, and a shortfall at a sample size of this order is real: for the same design ?seq_fwd_norm_mean reports a coverage of 0.938 from 40,000 replications where 0.95 was asked for. A run of this size cannot measure a shortfall of one percentage point; it shows the shape of the loop. The help pages of the classical procedures report runs of this kind with tens of thousands of replications, and vignette("special-cases-and-simulation", package = "SMSD") collects them.

Practical Guidance

  • Run the analysis at the width, confidence level, pilot size, and batch size the study will use, at every population value that is plausible, and under a skewed population as well as a normal one where the function offers the choice.
  • Use G = 10000 for anything that will be reported, give the seed, and report the Monte Carlo standard error with the coverage. Time the call with a small G first: at a narrow target ten thousand replications can take an hour or more.
  • Read coverage before relying on an interval at a planned width, and pct_hit_max_n before reading anything else when max_n was set.
  • When coverage is short of the confidence level, plan a narrower target, raise m_0, or both, and run the analysis again.
  • A preregistration or a proposal is the place for the resulting table: it tells a reviewer how large the study is likely to become and what the interval at the end can be trusted to do.

References
